utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We had a few procedural matters pending since yesterday. Two were pending, put perhaps it's better to first see whether we have now finished the examination of Mr. Krajisnik. There were a few matters which are at this moment verified, that is the verification of the translation of the day before yesterday, where Mr. Krajisnik said: That's not what I said, when he said: I didn't know the name, et cetera, et cetera. That is on its way to being verified on the basis of the audio. I do not have the results of that yet, but I'd like to consider Mr. Krajisnik still a witness until that has been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I checked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You checked it. Well, if you have anything to say about it, if you say: Well, I said this or I said that, of course, we'll verify it as well. But if you have any results to report, then you're free to do so, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last night I checked the video in relation to Mr. Kozic, so I can tell you the whole truth that I established, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm mainly interested in what you said at that time, because I take it that you verified what you said in this court that you didn't know the name, that the person was not identified. Was that -- was that different from what was put to you yesterday or what was put to you in the questions -- and there were two references to whether you were aware of the name of the person involved, were these correct quotes or is there any problem with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the quote, whether I said whether I knew about Mr. Kozic, it is correct that I then said that I did not know that it concerned Kozic. As for the second part of the quote, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second part, I'm just looking whether I can find it. I think it was your testimony of the 20th of June - is that correct? - the day before yesterday? Or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well -- yes -- no, but the first -- your answers to the question of Judge Hanoteau were on the -- was not yesterday, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The day before yesterday I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The day before yesterday. I'm trying to look at -- I'm searching for Kozic on the 20th of June and it doesn't give any result, which surprises me. But perhaps there's a wrong spelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 7th of June, that's when I was answering the questions put by Judge Hanoteau, the 6th and the 7th. I listened to that last night. That's what you said to me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I may be able to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll just look at my notes here for a minute. I believe Judge Hanoteau's questions were on the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And they started at 14:56:31, which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the problem is I've got pages in my LiveNote --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 15 was the page number, at least according to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll have to calculate because it starts at 26.000, so it should then be 44. Yes. I think I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the other reference is -- to Mr. Kozic occurred I think on the 7th of June in questioning that I -- questions I put to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 20th of June, well I didn't watch that, I didn't watch that recording. I only watched the 7th and the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just have a look. Yes, I think on the 20th of June it was mainly about the procedure that should have been followed, who was -- would have to report to whom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't view that. I'll review it this afternoon, but it was also part of the procedure on the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm now opening the 7th of June, and there -- could you give me one or two words that would help me searching because perhaps Kozic is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Kozic should be sufficient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm a bit concerned that the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Immunity, immunity that was being removed in the Assembly. That's what I said, and that the government should take measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to find "immunity." There's something with the search engine which is not -- yes. It was about your -- yes. I yesterday said that approximately 10 per cent, it was on the 7th. Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the text written out here, what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got it in front of me. You said, and that was part of the question put to you by Judge Hanoteau. You said: "There was no discussion about this, and this person was not identified as Kozic. Now I see it's Kozic -- well, probably it was. I don't know about this."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, that's what I said. That's what I said. That is the way I put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there was another reference that was -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that there is some references. The Judge or -- rather, no, the Prosecutor asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And you said: "Well, I'm telling you we had a session of the Assembly and then deputies in the corridors started discussing this. You Serbs are arming yourselves, and I didn't hear of any investigation or criminal charge or arrest or anything. I heard of nothing, and I didn't even know it was Kozic." That was the other reference to your knowledge on whether it involved Mr. Kozic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, too. I can tell you the sentence that I then uttered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I have two now. If you want to add one about your knowledge of Mr. Kozic, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that you said now is correct; however, the first reference was when I was asked by the Prosecutor: Tell us what are the two cases that you know of? And I said I didn't know anything about this -- oh, sorry, just a moment, please. One case in Bileca was being mentioned, and I know that a deputy was being mentioned. That's the first thing that I said. But really, after that I said that at that time that person was not identified as Kozic. Yesterday I said that it was only natural that I knew it was Kozic because I thought -- well, I mean, those two things do not coincide. He showed me that document from the newspapers, and as for the document I said that I did not know whether I read it, I mean whether I read the newspaper article because I was so resigned then. Maybe I read it. Maybe I read it and I thought that it wasn't correct. Also, what was said yesterday was not correct, that I had said that one has to go to the Assembly and that then the Assembly should refer this to the Office of the Prosecutor, as far as I understood it. I said that one had to go to the Assembly in order to remove a deputy's immunity; now that is correct. It's not for the Assembly to send this further on to the prosecutor's office so that the prosecutor would bring charges. I really do not recall the article that was shown to me yesterday, here, Karadzic. I don't remember that and I don't remember any contact with Kozic as far as this Bileca is concerned. Well, this is correct, that I said that at that time Kozic had not been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you are not contesting in this moment what is in the transcript of the 7th of June, but you're contesting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not, I'm not contesting that I said then that Kozic had not been identified then. Actually, that's what I thought, but I did say that there was this case in Bileca and I myself brought it up here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you say whether the interview -- the interview, as published, correctly reflects your words. That is something you are contesting. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not contesting it, but I don't know. Now, did he perhaps interpret this? Did he ask me whether I knew about Kozic and did I give this kind of answer? I don't know whether it's correct. I cannot say it's incorrect, but my position regarding paramilitary formations and the rest is exactly that way. I'm not challenging Karadzic's interview either, but I cannot recall. I've already said that, that I do not recall having read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now yesterday you referred a couple of times to material you gave us because I was wondering whether an Assembly -- BiH Assembly meeting took place in late May 1991. Overnight I tried to find it, but I didn't find it. Then I thought it might be in the material that you've provided to us. Yes. Could you tell us -- most important for me at this moment is what is the date of that Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I found this yesterday. The date is not the 24th, but rather the 21st and the 22nd of January -- no, May. Now, why I linked it to that Assembly I really don't know. I just linked it to the fact that I learned about it in relation to the Assembly, but the Assembly was on the 21st and 22nd of May. Now, did somebody talk about it later on, that can be checked, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because your testimony was that you learned about it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- when the Assemblymen were discussing rumours in the corridors, so no official report. I see now that there was an Assembly session at the 21st of May, which was prior to the incident, so it could not have been then that they discussed these rumours. Then there was one on the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could have been later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Krajisnik, let's go one by one. Then the next one was on the 22nd of May, and that was also prior to the incident, so they could not have discussed that at that moment. And then the next one was on the 12th of June, which was not only after the incident but well after the interviews as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right on everything. I can just give an interpretation. I certainly learned that around the Assembly or say after the Assembly, but I don't know. I had -- I know that it had to do with the Assembly. It wasn't on the 24th. I see that it was not then, but it had to do with the Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So chronologically the event takes place, and interview was published in which it is reported - right or wrong - that you knew about the name, that you were reported to have said that you had a personal -- personal conversation with Mr. Kozic. And only some two weeks after that, the first Assembly session, which would have allowed for the kind of rumours discussed in the corridors, as you described, could have been at least in the context of an Assembly session. That having been clarified --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said exactly that I had heard during the course of the Assembly, in the corridors, about this case. The Assembly was not held on the 24th. The only -- well, I said that I heard about it from the Muslim deputies. The only explanation I can give is that part of the deputies were there, later -- somebody must have told me about it, but I know it was around the Assembly. It could not have been apart from the Assembly. Perhaps that's the reason that problem was not at the Assembly session itself. I don't know. I didn't know when the Assembly was held -- I mean, I said indeed that it was during the course of the Assembly. Because sometimes deputies would stay on at some session of the other Chamber or some commission or whatever, I don't know. I said that I heard about it from the Muslim deputies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You clearly said not only that they discussed it, but also that that was the moment you learned about it. I remind you to your answer on the 7th of June, after we had some exchange on whether it was an extra-parliamentary discussion. You said: "At that Assembly, that is to say in this environment, I heard about this, that the MPs amongst themselves were mentioning this case, and that is when I learned of it."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least there was no Assembly session between the event itself and the interview that was published, and I think even Mr. Karadzic's interview was prior to the 12th of June. Okay. This matter has been sufficiently clarified, unless there is any questions the parties would like to put to Mr. Krajisnik in this respect. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I promised you that you would have an opportunity -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as indicated yesterday, I had a few matters to raise in connection with the Court's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't know if the Court was moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm again ignoring -- that's -- Mr. Tieger, apologies. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Further cross-examination by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few matters to raise in connection with some of the questions raised by the Bench. I expect that this will be brief. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, on Friday Judge Hanoteau asked you in connection with the issue of international allegations and information generally about prisoners and camps whether you, as president of the Assembly, could have undertaken an initiative in connection with those matters. And in that regard I'd like to turn to the Assembly Rules of Procedure which were -- which are in evidence as P64, P65 Treanor 9, tab 97, and if those could be distributed very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm sure you're familiar with these Rules of Procedure. Beginning at page 6 of the English and starting with article 55 of those rules, it provides for the establishment and operation of certain committees of the Assembly. If we turn to article 66, that reflects the committee for internal policy, the judiciary, and the administration. And -- although it's a relatively lengthy article compared to some of the others, it's not that long. And that committee exists, according to the rules, to discuss issues, including the organisation and work of the government, state administration and internal affairs, organisation and work of the courts, penal policy, court procedure, amnesty and pardon, further on down, attainment of equality of peoples and nationalities, and the freedoms, rights, and duties of man and citizens. And in connection with that, if we could also turn quickly to article 26, which provides that the president of the Assembly shall, among other things, submit an initiative for the debate on certain issues under the Assembly's jurisdiction, the president of the Assembly may also initiate debate on certain issues in the working bodies of the Assembly. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, in light of the breadth of the responsibilities of the committee for internal policy, the judiciary, and administration and the powers and responsibilities of the president of the Assembly in connection with the working bodies of the Assembly, it appears that the -- that you, as president of the Assembly, would have been in a position to undertake an initiative in connection with the allegations, information, charges, rumours about prisoners and camps. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes, but not in the sense that you mean. And this commission is not in charge of the things that you understand it to be in charge of. It only discusses material within the scope of its own work and prepares material for sessions of the Assembly, although commissions did not really work properly, they were established at a later date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, of course it's a little difficult for me to know exactly what your understanding of the sense that I mean this. So let me clarify it slightly. It -- this -- these provisions would place you -- would have placed you in a position at that time to undertake an initiative within the Assembly to determine whether the -- there was -- whether there was any basis for the charges of the international community concerning the arbitrary detention, maltreatment, and expulsion of non-Serbs and other aspects related --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem with this line of questioning - and that explains to some extent the apparent difficulties on Mr. Krajisnik's part in grappling specifically and precisely with the question - is that there's been a leap from the -- simply the wording of the rules containing an indication as to the circumstances in which the president of the Assembly may initiate these steps and the scope of the matters in question on which that might actually be done. And that's buried in Mr. Tieger's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He needs -- with respect, he needs to deal specifically with Mr. Krajisnik with those intermediate steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the second question or the first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the problem is the problem was buried there in the first question but it hasn't been resolved. What's happening is that difficulty with the first question -- and I waited to see whether that was actually causing any difficulty for Mr. Krajisnik in grappling with it, and in my submission it is apparent that it is, that leap which was made in this first question of this line of questioning is causing problems and it needs to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, with respect, I don't think there's any confusion at all. I put to Mr. Krajisnik that these provisions would have placed him in a position to undertake those steps. He said: Well, not in the sense you meant. I said: Well, here's the sense that that was meant, and he's in a position to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question then was whether article -- I take it that you're referring to article 66? Whether article 66 would put you in a position to undertake an initiative in connection with the allegations Mr. Tieger mentioned. If you could please answer that question without referring to anything else than the text of that question so that we are not responding to a possible understanding of what Mr. Tieger meant. Let's just focus on what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it not article 26 rather than article 66? Otherwise I think we may fall into confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a combination, Your Honour. Article 66 is the -- provides for the work of that particular committee; article 26 talks about the responsibilities and powers of the president in connection with --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Your Honour, but the -- it leads through -- article 26 is -- it's the -- if you like, it's the key provision but tied in with 66 in relation to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have been more precise and I should have referred to both. So whether on the basis of articles 26 considered also in relation to article 66, whether you were put in a position to take initiatives in connection with the allegations, information, charges, rumours, whatever about prisoners and camps. Could you please answer that question without interpreting what Mr. Tieger said else than what he literally said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for article 26, I could have put any question on the agenda and I could have started any initiative. Not 66, though, but only 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Krajisnik, His Honour Judge Orie inquired concerning Novi Privrednik and in that connection --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, sorry, let me explain this. It's very dangerous if I say that to you now and you say: All right, that's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the question is not fair then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you may add whatever you think -- unless you say it's important now to add anything to what you said, you said: I could have put any question on the agenda, I could have started any initiative, that's a clear answer to that question. But if you think you should add something to that -- without giving a long story --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- about -- so if you want to add --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. President, you keep giving me lectures every time. You've seen yesterday how difficult it is to answer questions. You don't have to instruct me three times. I do understand and I'm defending myself. That's not fair --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'll instruct you whenever the Chamber -- and I always discuss this with my colleagues. I instruct you whenever the Chamber thinks it -- such instruction is needed. Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Straight away and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from that I would like to add one thing first. Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber does understand that you are defending yourself if you are an accused, but at the same time you are a witness in which your duty to answer to questions is the primary duty, and of course the Chamber is not blind and is not deaf for the situation that being an accused -- that as a witness you would like to add matters, perhaps beyond -- that's very tempting, beyond what is specifically asked of you. But again, you'll have an opportunity to add anything to the last question put to you. Mr. Stewart -- one second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I would like to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Stewart intervened at that moment, to -- so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem lies in the fact that -- please, forgive me. If I can have one minute, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like Mr. Krajisnik -- I would like to speak on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf for a moment and ask Mr. Krajisnik's permission to take immediate precedence over him for a minute or two to speak on his behalf. It's this, Your Honour, and we -- I want Mr. Krajisnik to understand it, we appreciate that in the last two or three minutes Your Honour has very properly and very helpfully been seeking to protect Mr. Krajisnik and to be alert to his interests, and we thank you for that, Your Honour. We understand that what you said a few minutes ago was doing precisely that and I would like Mr. Krajisnik to appreciate that his counsel consider and submit that that is precisely what Your Honour was doing, which we naturally support. In relation to this line of questioning, where we were left -- and we slightly understand -- I hope we're not misreading Your Honour's mind. It's part of our job to read Your Honour's mind. We slightly understand what's happened is Mr. Krajisnik has confirmed at the end of that line of questioning that jurisdictionally under the rules he had a very, very wide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I finish, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted as a matter of fact to give an opportunity - I hope that's clear - to add whatever he would like to add to his confirming answer that under Rule 26 he would have the power to do so, but he wanted to add something. I was about to give him an opportunity to do that. If that's what you are seeking, that I would do, then you know if you would like to add anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour, I'm a hundred per cent with Your Honour. So I would like to finish, please, a simple thing very much in support of what Your Honour is saying just to ensure there's no confusion. Mr. Krajisnik has confirmed that jurisdictionally under the rules, basically, he said: Well, I could do pretty much anything I wanted. But then it's been left in the air as Mr. Tieger moves on to another area of questioning. What's been left in the air is the essential substance of the question which is well, actually, in those circumstances, in practice, that situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're doing now is suggesting what Mr. Krajisnik could have added. He could have want to add that he always confused article 26 with article 16 or he could -- whatever he could have said. I wanted to give him an opportunity to add whatever he wanted to add to that answer. It could be the things you are suggesting at this moment but it could --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting the answer, Your Honour. I don't understand why Your Honour is adopting this attitude towards me, Your Honour, since I've made it perfectly clear that we are at agreement on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you're telling the Court what in your view is incomplete in the answer what area is still not covered by the answer, and it could be anything. Mr. Krajisnik, you have an opportunity to add whatever you said when you said: Under 26 I could have taken any initiative. What would you like to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I launched hundreds of initiatives wherever it was appropriate. This particular article has been misinterpreted. Before that on the Presidency meetings where I was present, dozens of times material was given to the government on prisons and then it was forwarded to the parliament. A commission, which is only in charge of discussing material that had already been prepared is not well-placed or authorised to go out into the field to ascertain matters. That's within the purview of the government, office of the prosecutor, and other organs and the internal affairs. If there was a prison that was established and this was found out and it was placed on the agenda, I don't know what else I could have done. On the 11th of August Marinko Kontic said: We want to discuss prisons. I said - and this is something the Prosecution mentioned as their charge, saying that Krajisnik did not allow a debate on that to go on. I told them: We have a session the following day. Let's prepare material. We don't want to talk without having any material. But they didn't prepare the material before the 20th of August. You can't discuss matters at a meeting without have the necessary material. How can I discuss matters or launch an initiative if I don't have arguments in my hand? And that's the gist of the problem, that's the heart of the problem. I know exactly why this happened. Some matters were left unfinished in order for others to refer to that as an example of me not having done anything. And I did take steps to bring matters to a close, to achieve the end we wanted to achieve. There were other issues that I cannot possibly now talk about in one day. I wanted to tell you the whole truth, even if I were not accused I would be telling the truth. I launched an initiative, it was debated at the Presidency meeting, it was debated at the Ministry of the Interior, and what else could I have done? I mean, we could have had an initiative before us within the parliament, but then what would we have done with it? I would appeal to you to allow me to answer the questions fully to clear up matters because it's otherwise not fair to leave it unfinished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, of course we'll give you an opportunity to answer the questions. We would not give you an opportunity always to elaborate on whatever is, at least in your view, linked to the question, even if it's just a remote link. Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, I would not like to delve on this subject much longer because we've talked about it in length, but I would like to ask you a very, very simple question, and the question is as follows. Since there is rule 26, since it exists, and since you heard rumours, was it possible for you to tell the Assemblymen, without having prepared a report or anything like that: I heard rumours on arming, on detention camps, on what may happen inside those camps, and I would like to discuss those rumours. Were you able to do this, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without material, no. Not a single issue could have been discussed without material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Krajisnik, His Honour Judge Orie asked you about Novi Privrednik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that regard if I could have distributed and marked the next item.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a -- an article from Solobodna Bosna dated 28 November 1998, and we'll need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be, Your Honours, P1261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If there's another one, could we have it over here, please, if you've got another copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 5 of the English at the bottom, that is the last question and answer, and at page 00682616, the -- at the far left, the second question entitled "how much money did you give to the SDS?" Mr. Dukic stated the following, and I should indicate in addition that this is an interview with Rajko Dukic that appeared in Slobodna Bosna. And Mr. Dukic indicates that the giving money didn't work that way. Boksit as a company did not pay even half a dinar through its accounts to anybody. Our role was different. We had a representative office in Sarajevo in the Holiday Inn. Mirko Krajisnik was the head of that office. We had lots of business in Kakanj. Some of our machines were left there, et cetera. Then: "We formed two companies for the party at the time, Privrednik and Javnost. I took part with Miroslav Dahoja [phoen] and Dusko Kozic in founding Javnost. We acquired kiosks from donations and also equipment. Through Privrednik we carried out activities in the line with the firm's nature, such as in trade and fuel, and made a 3 per cent margin from which we financed the party. The party did not need too much money at that time." And there in a retrospective account of the purposes and activities of Privrednik, Mr. Dukic indicates its -- in part its activities and role and some of the participants. Is that correct, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- I've read that particular passage. Is that what you're referring to? Are you asking me to comment on what you've just read out?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, is that an accurate assessment by Mr. Dukic about the establishment of Privrednik and -- at least insofar as he describes it, its activities and role and participants?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Krajisnik was, between November and March, a representative of Boksit at Holiday Inn; that much is true. Before that he worked at Unioninvest. The two of them arranged this on their own. It is also true that Javnost existed and was established in the early says of the Serb Democratic Party in 1990, but its business was to publish a paper and they had kiosk. I'm not really privy to their business. Privrednik was not involved in this business in the 3 per cent and all that. As far as I was able to see that paper, Boksit signed and it was -- fuel was obtained through Boksit because that's where the office was at Holiday Inn, and the office there was shared by Privrednik and Boksit. Science Rajko Dukic was president of the Executive Committee of the SDS, this may have gone through some account, but I know that it was Boksit that was in charge of the business and Boksit gave this small margin of 3 per cent to the SDS. I may have been aware of that before, but it was recently that I saw this contract between Boksit and Mr. Karadzic on the issue of petrol. I think that the transactions went through Boksit and not through Privrednik because Privrednik in fact was operational for a month or two, I don't remember. It didn't even have its administration. I'm not even sure that it had a manager, but they had a transfer account. I know that much. The purpose of Privrednik's existence was probably to assist the SDS, but I don't think that Privrednik took any part in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Krajisnik, there was discussion about the selection of judges, and in particular the issue of the nomination of judges who were non-Serb. You pointed to some remarks by Mr. Karadzic concerning a certain percentage of nominees who were non-Serb and the awareness by Mr. -- by Dr. Karadzic and yourself, among others, that it was politically damaging in connection with relations with the international community to have a completely mono-ethnic structure. Now, in connection with the percentage -- and I should point out, too, that was a discussion that appeared to focus in -- to a large extent on the 19th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and you went through with Judge Orie a number of portion -- a number of portions of that session. In connection with the percentage non-Serb judges who were at issue in that session, non-Serb judges who were to be considered for the purposes we -- I just indicated, that percentage was 5 per cent, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was 5 per cent or not, but some percentage was discussed, that's true, and we always discussed it. And I can tell you why we discussed percentages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all negotiations there was discussion about the fact that once the agreement is reached, the make-up in the authorities should reflect the population make-up. Although there was a war on and although it was not really popular to have a Muslim as a judge, this was due to the war. That's why it was a problem. But we discussed that we had to have the exact ethnic make-up because we can't have a democratic state with only Serbs in it, and this had to do with the -- this was some -- this was part of the commitments we took in all the negotiating agreements. I know that there was 23 per cent of Muslims before the war on what is today the Republika Srpska. It doesn't matter whether it was 23 or 25. So this was the percentage that had to be reflected in the government and in all the other structures. This had always been a rule in Bosnia. The only difference would have been that the Serbs would have been in the majority, but this sort of make-up should have been reflected in the authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn quickly to page 13 of the English of the 19th Session and page 12 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court doesn't have the -- I don't know if the Court has the session handy, but I have copies to distribute, if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Mr. Popovic talking immediately before the vote taken on judges. I think this portion was looked at yesterday, the voting portion, when you read out everyone's name, surname, father's name, and nationality, but Mr. Popovic spoke immediately before that and he indicated that there were talks with the republic, Ministry of Justice, and an agreement that a per cent of judges of other nationalities proposed for appointment would be 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but if they discussed this, they probably thought that this should be the case because the same was true for the other side. This was more a political issue, but later on the percentage should have reflected the population make-up. This was probably just a political issue here, but not the final solution to the problem because in practice 5 per cent would not have worked. The percentage would have to increase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition, Mr. Krajisnik, yesterday in connection with the issue of selection of judges you said at one point that the situation had not ripened or matured because the issue of citizenship was not resolved, and I think that occurred at page 12, toward the bottom, at around line 23. I wanted to take a brief look at the handling of the citizenship issue to see if we can glean any insights into attitudes or positions toward potential Muslim judges or non-Serbs generally. At the 22nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held in late November 1992, that issue was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, 22nd Session is contained in tab 345. It should have been made available to the Court, and I'll direct the Court and Mr. Krajisnik to the appropriate pages. If we could turn to page 77 of the English at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And page 9706 of the become, Mr. Krajisnik, quickly moving into 9707. And that's Mr. Milojevic speaking. I believe we met him earlier in connection with the discussion of judges. And he's the first speaker as the discussion moves on to item 10 of the agenda, the citizenship bill. We can see that in the -- in your remarks just before Mr. Milojevic speaks. And then turning to page 78 of the English - it should be the bottom of page 9706 or the top of page 9707 - Mr. Milojevic raises two concerns about the citizenship bill. First he notes that it's -- article 1 of the constitution stipulates that Republika Srpska is the state of the Serbian people. And then in another place he notes and quotes, "citizens of Republika Srpska shall be granted citizenship of Republika Srpska, which means everybody. I think it should read 'Serbian. '" You then note: "That's a mistake. Feel free to correct it, Professor, so we can move on." Then he goes on to his second point. Second -- and I'll quote. "Second, the citizenship of Republika Srpska shall be acquired, among other things, by birth in the territory of Republika Srpska. This refers to all the Muslims and Croats we expelled. In reality, they are also citizens of Republika Srpska." So at this point -- unquote at the end of the words "Republika Srpska." So Professor Milojevic raises two problems in connection with the proposed citizenship bill. The first is the one stated about whether or not it should read "Serbian," which you address quickly in your comment; and the second is that it would have the contradictory and paradoxical effect of granting citizenship to all those Muslims and Croats who were expelled, and he raises both of those as problems. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He raised both these issues; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Perhaps I should have intervened earlier. As I said yesterday, and we are quite limited in our time; we have to stop now. The parties are invited to remain stand-by on from 12.00, and most likely we'll resume close to 12.30. Therefore, we'll have a break within these limits. --- Luncheon recess taken at 10.45 a.m. --- Luncheon recess taken at 10.45 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume. The parties may have been wondering why we were so vague about when to resume, et cetera. If I say that this must be a wonderful day for dentists, in the plural, that could give a clue. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just before we briefly adjourned, I had directed your attention to the remarks of Mr. Milojevic at the 22nd Session concerning citizenship and the -- for your benefit and the benefit of the Court that was -- those were found at page 78 of the English and page 9706 and 9707 of the B/C/S. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it last time. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of the concerns expressed by Mr. Milojevic, the bill was sent back to the committee for further review, along with the proposal that Mr. Milojevic and Mr. Radovic, I believe, provide assistance in improving the law. Is that correct? And I find that reflected on page 79 of the English and that's 9707 through 9708 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put this in my bag and I can't find it. I'll try -- well, it's not here. Never mind. I cannot find it, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can certainly provide you with an additional ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And my question was simply whether or not it's correct that as a result of the concerns expressed by Mr. Milojevic the bill was sent back for further review and improvement.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the main reason. Citizenship of Republika Srpska is something that I understood to be like before the war in Yugoslavia, that is under B, whereas under A you would have what was the former Yugoslav citizenship. That would have the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a political settlement been found. So lawyers should have looked into it and found the best possible solution. Although his contribution certainly led to it not being adopted as well as others who were against it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in connection with the issue of -- or the possibility of Muslim judges, one of the issues involved in that was that there was some question about the conditions under which Muslims would be citizens at all, and therefore qualified to serve as judges?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Citizenship of Republika Srpska or Serb citizenship was like any republican citizenship, that is to say of a region perhaps, in Western terms. There were different participation in the discussion here. People disagreed, so then it had to go back in order to be brought in a court with various conventions and what have you not, because discussing this kind of thing with a man who's not a lawyer at the Assembly session would certainly be a waste of time. Of course Muslims could be citizens, if I can put it that way, of Republika Srpska if they are from Republika Srpska. Of course. Later on they voted, too. So that is, no doubt, correct. However, it was put differently here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can find the final text that was adopted. Probably it exists somewhere, the text as it was finally adopted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm -- in any event, irrespective of the final text that was adopted, it's fair to say that during the time that the selection of -- or the possibility of selecting Muslim judges was being discussed at, for example, the 19th Session, specifically the 19th Session, there was still a question about the conditions in which Muslims or non-Serbs might become citizens of Republika Srpska, and therefore a question about their entitle to serve as judges. I think that's reflected, in fact, in Mr. Milojevic's remarks at the 19th Session at page 15 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that there was a discussion and that there was that problem -- or rather, to resolve another problem. And there was this discussion - how should I put it? - that made the political situation impossible, one that made it impossible to resolve that problem, that is. Although that was unfounded, it is nevertheless true because they were against the Muslims being judges because there was a war going on, on the other side there weren't any Serbs, and so on. That is why they refused to vote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one final issue I'd like to turn to, Mr. Krajisnik. You were asked -- or during the course of the discussion you had with the Judges about camps and prisoners and, in particular, the widespread dissemination of information about the camps in Prijedor following the entry of the international media into those camps in early August 1992, you made reference to an allegation that the footage of the prison camps in Omarska was in some manner -- I think your words were "stage-managed."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I have. That's what it looks like, that people are outside the barbed wire rather than inside. The Defence has it. That's in Trnopolje. And there is a statement of a man who says: We are here voluntarily, we can leave, we can go out, we can come back. All of that is on that cassette. They were recording it, so it seemed that they were behind a wire fence. The Defence should find it and show it to you. That's what I saw here. I didn't see it before or afterwards and the thin man is there, and he is making a statement. You've got it all here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're making reference, Mr. Krajisnik, to the allegations by a journal called "Living Marxism," and specifically by a journalist called Thomas Deichmann. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be quite honest. I do not remember who the journalist was. The best thing would be to have a look at the video cassette, and then you can see who filmed it -- and also there was this criticism against the journalist who was given an award for this false information, as they had put it. I'm telling you what I saw. You can have a look yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just three things, Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, those allegations by Deichmann in "Living Marxism" weren't published until 1997, so they had no impact an your consideration in camps in Prijedor or elsewhere in 1992, did they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I got information from people who had been there. I didn't see that footage until I came here, to prison, that footage that criticised this, rather. So I hadn't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, setting aside all other evidence relating to camps in Prijedor, including the footage taken by numerous journalists and media outlets, including the United Nations Commission of Experts' reports; including the testimonies of hundreds of witnesses, detainees; including the judgements in several cases that focussed specifically on those camps, including the adjudicated facts. Setting all that aside, you're also aware, aren't you, that the journalist who entered the camps filed a libel suit against Living Marxism for the allegations that that footage was in some manner stage-managed or doctored, and they won a judgement of several hundred thousand dollars because the allegations that the footage was in some manner doctored or stage-managed were found to be untrue and found to be libel. Let me distribute these documents. This is in English, Mr. Krajisnik, but I'll read you the pertinent portions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just say: Don't bother. I heard the same thing. I heard the same thing, that journalists filed a suit, yes, that's true. I'm just telling you what I saw. I can also tell you the rest that I know about journalists. I haven't read this, but I know -- I heard that allegedly he had been taken to court. The best thing would be to view the footage, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask at this very moment about Trnopolje because we are talking about Trnopolje -- at least I understand the footage was filmed at Trnopolje. Mr. Tieger, you said: Apart from the hundreds of witnesses, et cetera, et cetera, the adjudicated facts. Would it be of major use at this moment to go into great detail into a footage of which true or false would not -- which, as far as I understand, a footage which was not the main basis of the establishment of facts in other cases where many, many witnesses have been heard. So would this really have such an impact that we'd have to go through it now? Because the Defence is fully aware that if you want to attack adjudicated facts, it should be done thoroughly because it's the result of a -- of taking a lot of evidence. I can imagine that Mr. Krajisnik, being aware of allegations that this footage was not -- was framed, more or less, that he wants to draw our attention to it. But it would not be -- I would say he does this now as a witness. Let's wait and see whether the Defence launches an attack on this, adjudicated facts. I haven't heard anything about it until now. Did -- this, most likely, would be an element in such an attack. It would then have to overcome all the evidence that was taken into consideration by the other Chambers. So I wonder whether it really assists us in going into great detail, even telling us what the outcome is of other court cases. Of course, I see that it's an English court, which of course would be perhaps of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take the Court's guidance and I have a couple of additional questions related to this topic, but not on -- but that won't implicate -- that won't run afoul of the Court's suggestions in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've seen -- at least by putting these questions you've drawn the attention of the Defence and the answers have drawn the attention of the Defence to such allegations by the journalist, Mr. Deichmann. Let's see what is done on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll defer on any -- if I'm seeking any number on that, in light of the Court's guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just confirm we've been listening attentively to everything that has just said, on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll retain it, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the fact is that everyone in the Assembly knew that the treatment of prisoners in the camps in Prijedor and other Bosnian Serb detention facilities was deplorable and that those who left detention did so in a debilitated condition, which required a period of recovery and recuperation after their release.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me when it is that you thought that the deputies knew about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's begin with the -- perhaps a more specific example. We had an opportunity the other day to see the condition of the prisoners who were shipped from Bratunac to Visoko through Pale. And as we could see in the video, the prisoners were battered. Some could scarcely walk, and others could barely sit up. Members of the Assembly by the summer -- within a few months of that, at any rate, knew that those prisoners, the ones who had been transported via Pale from Bratunac required some period of recovery, restoration, recuperation as a result of their treatment in confinement.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one knew. I didn't know either in what condition these prisoners were in Pale -- if you're talking about Pale. You started talking about Prijedor. You should have told me when you were talking about Prijedor. As for Pale, I didn't know in what conditions they were in and the MPs didn't know either. The MUP drove them off and finished this job within two days. I didn't even know about it. I heard about it then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get back to Prijedor camps in just a moment, but I had mentioned both the detention facilities in Prijedor and elsewhere. Let's turn then, if we can, to the 20th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and look at remarks of Mr. Radic. That was the Assembly held on the 14th and the 15th of September, 1992, found at page 45 of the English and page 47 of the B/C/S. Now, on page 45 of the English, Mr. Radic's remarks take up the bottom half of the page, and in approximately the middle of those comments you'll see a reference to 11.500 Serbs in Ilijas and 70.000 Muslims in Visoko and Breza and then a reference to 400.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what Mr. Radic told the Assembly on that occasion was: "The government ordered us to allow passage to 400 Balija to Visoko, where they recuperated and they are now fighting against us." "Where they recuperated," Mr. Krajisnik, wasn't that a reference to their condition following their period of detention, the condition that we had an opportunity to see on that video?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe he said it but the point was that they were sent to the front against them. Those who were that sick should have been taken to hospital rather than to the front line. I do not remember this contribution to the discussion, but I'm just interpreting it now. He was criticising this. We are supposed to release them and then they're sending these same people to fight against us. I don't know what this recovery is supposed to mean. Psychologically? Physically? Were they mistreated? The point is that somebody let them go and implicitly it is being stated that the other would be released, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not the only time that someone's speaking about prisoners who were detained and held in Bosnian Serb detention facilities took for granted that all the members of the Assembly would understand that a period of recovery and recuperation was necessary. So why don't we look next to the comments of Mr. Srdic at the 24th Session of the Assembly held on the 8th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be found at page 29 of the English and at page 22 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There on page 29 Mr. Srdic's remarks take up the first three-quarters of the page at approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if the Court will look down about two-thirds of the way through his remarks you'll see the number "5.000."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here again Mr. Srdic is registering the complaint that the Bosnian Serbs shouldn't have let militarily age -- or militarily capable people go. And he says: "Just three, four months ago we were absolute masters in the war. What are we facing now? We are facing it because we played a fair game and in the interests of peace in the house, hoping for the well being of the Serb people. We let go 5.000 militarily capable people from our collection centres who meanwhile recovered and were trained in Karlovac and other places in Croatia and are now ready and waiting to strike again at our Serb people." And he attributes this to UNPROFOR and the international -- and the European Community. That, Mr. Krajisnik, is another reference reflecting the widespread understanding that the people who were confined in the camps in Prijedor and the people who were confined in camps elsewhere were treated in such a manner that it would be necessary for them to recover from the effects of that treatment before they could do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain something. You see this figure here, 5.000, and the reception centre. I testified about that. They were released from Trnopolje. That is why it was being said about Trnopolje all the time. I mean, it is not my objective to challenge this, whether Trnopolje is a reception centre or a prison; I'm just telling you what kind of information I was receiving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik. No, Mr. Krajisnik. You're supposed to answer the question. You're not supposed to elaborate on whether Trnopolje -- the question simply was whether where it says: "Who meanwhile recovered," whether that's a reference to their bad state of health. That's the question. Nothing else. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. How can he know what they agreed on in Karlovac? He's just guessing. It was September and then January 1993. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, how Mr. Srdic could know something that happened elsewhere is not something to speculate on. If you know that this is a reference to their bad state of health, tell us that it is a reference, that you would agree with Mr. Tieger. If you said as you said in your last answer: I have no idea whether they've got to recover psychologically, physically, I have no idea, how could I know, then you say: I cannot confirm that this is a reference to their bad state of health. That's a simple question. So please consider it and don't elaborate on matters which are not in the core of the question. At least start with answering the question. Please, is it a reference -- "who meanwhile recovered," is that a reference to the bad state of health of these people, yes or no? Or whatever you could say about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Possibly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, it's not an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is an answer. Of course it is an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not an answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if I say it is an answer, then I don't want any comment from you to say that it is an -- that it's not an answer. Yes? Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe what the question essentially is. The question is really whether there was a widespread understanding, such as Mr. Tieger suggests. That's the nub of the question. It isn't really the interpretation directly of the words. That's what the question is and that's -- I suspect Mr. Tieger would confirm that's essentially his question and that's what Mr. Krajisnik -- I say nothing about answers, Your Honour, but that's the question that Mr. Krajisnik is essentially being asked to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It could be -- I understood the question to be -- but let's -- let's give Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- full opportunity. I understood it to be in order to establish whether this was well-known, yes or no. Let's first look at the words that were spoken and let's see what these words mean and then in order to -- if they -- if, for example, Mr. Krajisnik would have said: Who meanwhile recovered, well what was just to say that it was only psychologically, so therefore -- because nothing to do with diseases, it had got nothing to do with malnutrition, et cetera, then at least we would know how these words are understood and then, of course, we'd further hear questions and answers about whether everyone heard that, how many people were present. I mean, that's how I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Your Honour, the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do say the question is impossible to interpret other than essentially in the way that I suggest because it makes -- it makes an implicit assumption -- it's based on the assumption that there was a widespread understanding, et cetera, and it is asking the witness whether this statement reflects that widespread understanding. So it -- the essential point in this is to see, first of all, whether the witness acknowledges that there was -- well, I won't go any further, Your Honour. Your Honour will say I'm crossing from question to answer, so I will stop there. But, Your Honour, it's clear that that is the nub of the point that's being put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if there was any assumption in your question, Mr. Tieger, might be, and which is in my view, and apart from the leading character, of course, allowed in -- well, it's now apart -- it's not cross-examination, really, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, I accept that. I accept that. I accept it's cross-examination and Mr. Tieger can lead in the usual way. I don't dispute that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there is another matter, that as we have adjudicated facts about the -- about the health condition of those in the camps which has not been frontally attacked, has not thoroughly been attacked. So if that is part of the question, say: This is a reference to those facts, because that's where we might disagree, Mr. Stewart. You say it's a reference to the wide-known -- that these facts were widely known, whereas I understood it just as a reference to these facts to start with. Mr. Tieger, you've had a lot of interpretations of your questions. 17

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, Your Honour, I think that the Court asked a very direct and specific question, which was answered -- I -- from as far as I can see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- addresses the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- issue of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- the issue and I have -- let me just check very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Stewart, whether you have any questions depended on whether there were any questions from the Prosecution. Unfortunately overnight I had no time to reconsider the question, whether who was first to ask, but we are now in the situation as we are. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's academic right now, Your Honour, because I don't. So there's no need for us to debate that issue, on which, no doubt, we will reserve our position if and when it ever comes up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I will have found the time to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour -- if may I say, Your Honour, I had Mr. Mandic's evidence here in court for obvious reasons yesterday, and the way this situation was dealt with in relation to Mr. Mandic does give a very clear pointer, the Defence suggests, as to the way in which it should be dealt with. But, Your Honour, it may never arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber promised you to give an opportunity an add whatever you think is important to the answers you've given already to the questions and also to draw our specific attention to documents you presented and from which, until now, we have not heard from the parties that they wanted to adopt them -- at least the few ones that were not yet in evidence. I also note that this is a rather technical problem that some of these documents, especially in the earlier stages, were provided with provisional exhibit numbers. So we might -- when we go through the list at a later stage, we might review whether they should be on the list at all. Mr. Krajisnik, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm quite handicapped, actually, because I was looking for a quotation from the 6th and 7th of June all night long, but at any rate I will try to explain further some of my answers. First of all, I wish to say that I stated here without any further explaining that in the negotiations there were negotiators who were in favour of an Islamic state. I was then asked whether I had stated that. I provided one of the documents which shows that a study was being produced. This is the document from Mr. Muhamed Filipovic's book. There you have all the information. My explanation that not the -- it wasn't the entire delegation that negotiated with us that was in favour of a Muslim state; rather, this view was advocated by some individuals. And I gave an example here. You can find the document among the paper I -- the paperwork I gave here. The second issue, which I don't know why it was overlooked, Mr. Djokanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just deal with the first matter. Is it in dispute that among those negotiating that there have been -- or there may have been individuals who favoured an Islamic or a Muslim state?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, when you put it that way I suppose there would not be a dispute that there may have been. I have not personally seen a reflection in any documentation that a member of a negotiating team took that position. I don't want to make a big dispute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. At the same time we heard the witness, Mr. Krajisnik, tell us that there was. I've heard no further questions on the matter. Therefore, I thought that it was not contested that there may have --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a phrase. I don't know whether it exists. I do not contest, although I have no knowledge on the matter. That means that you would -- as the Germans do it in court, they call it a "wahrunterstellung," which means that they just assume that it is true. Whether it is true or not we make it -- it could be true, but we're not making any issue out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to have to learn that expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is "wahrunterstellung" which is an assumption of truth and it avoids a lot of evidentiary exercises. So if one party states something, the other says: I don't know, but I'm willing to accept that it would be the truth and therefore we know -- we're taking no point on it. Is that the case as far as individuals in the negotiation team in favouring an Islamic state?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is certainly correct the state, Your Honour, that we have taken no point on that and the evidence stands as it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we should avoid that further efforts are made to have documents translated, unless it's in English. I don't think it -- it doesn't assist very much. But, Mr. Stewart, I'm also looking at you, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "wahrunterstellung" interpolation to what Your Honour's just said. But we don't disagree at all with what Your Honour has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second issue. Mr. Djokanovic presented an accusation here, rather, that he had familiarised the leadership with the atrocities that had happened in Zvornik. I presented here an excerpt from September 1993, which is an Assembly session, containing his statement where he clearly stated that no genocide was committed in Zvornik, and he said so clearly in front of the entire Assembly and said that any such allegations were unfounded. I presented this because I wanted to let you know that he had never informed anyone about what had happened in Zvornik. Let me just say in support of this, on the 10th of June, 1992, he came to Pale; and on the 12th he went out in the field, from where he returned on the 16th. On the 30th of June, he was in Zvornik with Karadzic and Mladic attending a meeting. There were all presidents of municipalities there, and he could have discussed the matter with all of them and resolved the entire Zvornik issue. In 1993 he was a cabinet minister and he could have raised all these issues there and take any and all steps to investigate into these crimes. Thirdly, the military Supreme Court was seated in Zvornik. If all the ears were deaf to him, he could have knocked on that door there and say: I am a commissioner for such-and-such issues and I wish to report these crimes. I believe that he gave up the whole matter because he was afraid that at the end he would be found guilty of that all. Please take a look at this excerpt from the September 1993 Assembly session, and there you will see what he stated in front of all the deputies. And he stated what I have just said. Can I now move on to the third issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to find out. Is the September 1993 Assembly session, is that in evidence already? I haven't got the whole of the lists here anymore, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Tieger. I hope that you'll forgive me that not -- knowing from every single session, whether it's in evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I -- we're looking right now, but I think the great likelihood, Your Honour, is that at most excerpts from that session would be, to the best of my recollection at this point, Sessions 1 through 24 are fully in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in respect to other -- with respect to other sessions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Tieger doesn't say that that's the session. Mr. Tieger is explaining what sessions are in their totality in evidence, and then he says --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that it's most likely only an excerpt. And then, of course, the question is whether this excerpt is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's my best estimate at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, Mr. Krajisnik, have you identified in the -- do we know the exact date in September, which might make it more easy to identify the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have it there with other papers because I annexed that particular page and highlighted the text, together with all the other material I submitted to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll try -- we'll ask Mr. Registrar to see whether he can identify on this index as far as it has been prepared now, whether there is any 1993 -- September 1993 Assembly session. So if it's not translated yet, it would be -- at least contain the word "Skupstina".

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We may have some other information but -- sorry, excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, this -- we're talking about September 1993. The range of sessions that Mr. Tieger mentioned, Sessions 1 to 24, has being fully in evidence that only takes us up to January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what Mr. Tieger said, in my view, for this period of time we have the full in evidence -- the totality of the minutes, apart from sometimes a few missing pages, we have everything in evidence. So if it would be from another period, we might have only an excerpt, if at all, in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I understand. I see -- so, in a sense, the mention of Sessions 1 to 24 was a bit extra information not directly related to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's what threw me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it -- this particular session - and there may be others in the post-1992/early-1993 period - was introduced in full as P64A, tab 39 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In full?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the information I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And also, Your Honour, P65, tab 221.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'll go to it -- yes, please go on, Mr. Krajisnik. I'll try to find Mr. Djokanovic's statement in P64A, tab 39. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to your question that -- whether I proposed that the discussion about unifying military and civilian judiciary be placed on the agenda, I would like to refer you to two matters. The discussion held at that particular Assembly meeting concerned the merging of civilian and military health services. This was in return for further discussion. When it came for the matter to be discussed that the civilian judiciary should be subordinated -- or rather, the military should be subordinated to the civilian, it was said that this was not in accordance with the constitution or with the law. You can see that I said that this particular initiative would have to be returned for further review.
