There's this first sentence where he says that it's not either in accordance with the constitution or with law and that it had to be further worked on, because as it stood then it would have required both the constitution and the relevant law to be amended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The discussion here was that on the 14th of May, 1992, a large attack was launched by the Serb armed forces on Sarajevo. I didn't know at the time, but it was asked as to what Krajisnik had done to prevent this. I myself didn't know where I was on the 14th of May, but the other day you were able to see on the basis of Mr. Zimmermann's book that on the 12th of May we were attending an Assembly meeting at Banja Luka. On the 13th of May we attended the festivities organised by their police. And on the 14th of May we were flying on a plane and Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic attended a meeting with Mr. Zimmermann. I was with my family waiting for them to come back to the meeting in order for us to return to Pale. That is why the meeting was chaired by Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Stanisic, which proves that I wasn't at Pale at the time of the event. May I proceed, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that on the 23rd of August, 1992, I could not have attended the Presidency session. And I also said that a couple of days before that date and after that date I wasn't in Pale. It was quite rightly that the Prosecution led the evidence that on the 22nd of August I had received representatives of SRNA. I myself located that piece of news, and I also included that together with the report from the military medical academy of Belgrade, where it says precisely that on the 20th Pale was bombed, that on the 21st I gave a statement to the VMA concerning my wife, and that on the 23rd at 6.00 in the morning she passed away. I can't explain the origin of that piece of news, but how could I have been on the 21st in Belgrade and then return to receive SRNA and then from there go back to Belgrade to look for a coffin and then go through a shower of shells in order to have her buried? On the 22nd, I was most definitely not in Pale; I was in Belgrade all that time because she was in a coma for three or four days. I was waiting to see whether she was going to die or live. And you have the documentation -- I obtained the documentation from the VMA, and there you have the chronology of events, what sort of statement I gave, and so on and so forth. I'm really sorry to have to use these resources to show you that I wasn't at that Presidency session on the 23rd of August. I have all the material, and it is there for you to look at it. May I carry on, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, but I'd like to add that I think, from what I remember, that although -- of course your presence in -- outside Belgrade was put to you but not major follow-up was given to it in further questioning, which the Chamber considered to be a wise thing to do in view of the circumstances at that time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I only wanted to say that journalists can also make mistakes. That's what I wanted to say because I could not have been in Pale on the 22nd. There was Mr. Mazowiecki's report, and I took a negative view of his report. I would like to state one thing. I assess the report to be partial. He says that he was in Sarajevo and that he was unable to visit prisons. I documented here that he was at Viktor Bubanj and he could have gone to Silos, Hadzici. We insisted that he visited the area, and he did not. There were people who had spent five years in prison there. I wish to say that I don't think he did that deliberately, but he was planted this by someone and he wrote his report accordingly. That is why my assessment of his report was that it was not objective because he merely went on to explain what was going on, on the Serb-held territory. I do not wish to challenge that, but he should have stated in his report what was going on, on the other side as well. There was mention of the shelling of Sarajevo on the 28th of May. I really didn't know that it was bombed or why. I can only tell the Trial Chamber, if it will be helpful, that Pofalic is mentioned in the phone call where Mladic said: "Fire upon Pofalici." You've heard that. I wish to say that on the 15th of May Muslims committed a great pogrom of Serbs at Pofalici where his family resided. They either killed or expelled Serbs from that suburban area. And at that time, barracks were being relocated. I'm not justifying this attack on Sarajevo at all. I condemn it. But I'm merely trying to tell you that these may have been the reasons why Sarajevo was bombed, although, of course, they cannot be justified in any way. The next issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I maybe just interrupt you for one second. Mr. Tieger, I tried to verify the Assembly session in September 1993 Mr. Krajisnik was referring to. You said it would be P64A, tab 39. I there find nine pages only Mr. Gvero speaking. Then you refer to P65, tab 221. There I find 25 out of 466 pages -- at least on my screen, which of course should be verified in the originals. So therefore a full transcript is -- as far as I can see now under these numbers not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I say that was -- in fact, that was the exact same point that I was just discussing with Mr. Josse, as Your Honours, but we have done the same check and come up happily -- well, happily or unhappily with exactly the same result as Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, the evidence as such -- and certainly also these 25 pages would not deal with any statement given by Mr. Djokanovic at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the misinformation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I take it that since the evidence says that it's 25 out of 466 pages that they are somewhere, because otherwise you couldn't say there are 466 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's fully translated to the best of my knowledge. We can introduce it -- I mean, at this point I'm at the Court's disposal, but it's available for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it it's in a text format as well, so it might be an easy thing to find - I think it was Mr. Djokanovic speaking - or even search for the words "genocide," because Mr. Krajisnik said there was no genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We have the ERN numbers of the -- well, this is the B/C/S. The B/C/S pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I take it that with this help that -- the parties -- and I'm calling upon both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could easily find perhaps the -- the reference Mr. Krajisnik made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I have no doubt about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the only remaining question is that the Prosecution will also conduct a contextual review to see if additional portions need to be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that goes without saying. We would allow that to the Defence, so we would allow that to the Prosecution as well. Mr. Krajisnik, please proceed. You see we are trying to give as quickly follow-up to the matters you raise as we can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric's statement has been quoted here where in an Assembly session at Zvornik -- or rather, that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Mandic, as ministers, were well-informed because they were always in the office of the president of the parliament and president of the republic. I'm asserting that this isn't true, but I understand why he put it that way. The government was perhaps some 10 to 15 kilometres away from our seat at Pale. When I checked the attendance by Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic - and I mean their attendance of government sessions - I realised that they were absent from a large number of meetings. Mr. Djeric probably thought that at that time they were with the president of parliament or president of the republic or president of the Presidency, that is. I can't recall -- or rather, there were very few meetings where I met them. There was no reason for them to inform the president of the republic or president of the Assembly and not inform the Prime Minister on some matters. The problem lay in the separation of the government from the Assembly and the Presidency, and in several places in the minutes the Prime Minister stated that they had to have a joint meeting with the president of the Assembly and the president of the republic in order to be better informed. I, on my part, believed that I should have been informed by the government on many matters. Perhaps because of this lack of information, he believed that we were in possession of some information that he was not, although this wasn't true. The fact that these two institutions were located at different places he -- led him to the impression that we were informed of matters that they were not. There was this commission that was set up, and this led to resentment which escalated into a conflict that had grave consequences, and I'm referring to the toppling of the government. Mr. Tieger, as well as others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, I just want to try to focus you on what kind of evidence this Chamber would very much like to hear. I do understand -- although it's a long story, I do understand that you say: The fact that we are in one building and the fact that Mr. Djeric was in a totally different place might be relevant facts for creation of a confusion that when he would see the one person in the one building that he would also see the other one. I mean, you start giving a lot of reasoning and you are telling us that the -- that this led him to the impression. That's all -- well, let's say -- I do understand that you want to draw our attention to that, but a lot of the reasoning is not of great assistance to us; however, drawing our attention to facts which could declare a confusion certainly is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said just now is what the two of them said, Mandic and Stanisic, at the same session, both of them. Perhaps I did not put it very well that this led him to, and so on and so forth. That is what the two of them said at that session. That indicates what their statements were at that particular session, where Djeric said what he said -- I mean what I said a few minutes ago. But let me move on then. Mr. Treanor and other witnesses, too, said that a session of the Assembly was held on the 11th of August, 1992, and that Marinko Kontic, MP, supported by Nikola Erceg asked to have a debate on prisoners. That was five days after the discussion that took place at the Presidency meeting, when I attended that consultative meeting. The conclusion was that Krajisnik did not allow a debate on prisoners. I would like to draw your attention to the following lines at that session. There were several proposals, and then I said: Let the government prepare this material for tomorrow. Let's not discuss it without any material, and then we'll continue the 19th Session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember at what page we find that? It was -- you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't got it in front of me, but it's at the beginning of the session when the agenda was being set, Marinko Kontic, and then later on I explained what happened to amendments to the agenda. I said so very nicely: We can discuss it tomorrow, just prepare the material for all the items that had not had prepared materials. I can underline all of it and bring it in for you tomorrow. I didn't know that today, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, tomorrow you are not a witness anymore, I take it. But of course there's nothing wrong if tomorrow Defence counsel for the defence of Mr. Krajisnik would inform us about what portion of -- of the Assembly minutes were referred to in their view.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agenda, establishing the agenda, that's where referred to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind you that the government did not have this material on the 26th of August, that is to say later. Prisoners were discussed at a closed session, I think it was the 46th Session, in Banja Luka. At the same time, this is a response to the Prosecutor. From the month of August, from the first indications onwards, it was known that the conditions for the prisoners were improper, August 1992 onwards. Constant attempts or efforts were being made to improve their condition. I'm not denying that. Somebody was always in charge of improving this. I wasn't contesting it. I just said: Give me the time-frame. Then the Presidency issued an order to disband the prisons, to improve conditions, the government passed a decision. All of that is correct. That's why I said that before that we didn't know, but from then onwards all measures were taken. I am not going to say anything that was not true, but you just didn't let me explain. Whenever anyone said anything, the task was to improve conditions. As Srdjo Srdic said: Please, they were released in August 1992, these 5.000. And he says in January they, having recovered, are now supposed to go back. That is what I mentioned when Karadzic had let 5.000 prisoners go free after the London Conference. He did it on his own, and then he said that the Muslims would later release Serb prisoners, too, as he said from the reception centre. Another thing that was constantly insisted upon here was that there was an expanded Presidency. I said quite resolutely on several occasions that there never was an expanded Presidency. I know it did not exist. Secondly, I never would have agreed to be in an illegal body. I would have asked the Assembly to adopt that. I provided a document to you -- actually, it has to do with the 17th of December, 1992, when the Assembly changed the constitution and annulled a decision on municipal commissioners. That is to say that a decision was made on municipal Presidencies and then it was abolished. A decision was made on municipal commissioners, and it was abolished. No decision was ever passed on an expanded Presidency in an immediate threat of war, which would have been according to the constitution where I would have had certain powers and responsibilities. And such a decision was never annulled. The constitution was amended and there was only three members of the Presidency. They got different functions. The Presidency and two vice-presidents. If I were that important, Karadzic should have said: Don't change Krajisnik. Let him be the third member, whatever. I just stayed on as the president of the Assembly, like before. I provided a document that things cannot simply go without saying that I'm a member of the Presidency. I have documents here as to how they worked in the Muslim part. They passed a decision on the basis of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was a yardstick for us, too. Where it says that in case of immediate threat of war, the Presidency is expanded in order to include the president of the Assembly, the Prime Minister, and the commander of the Territorial Defence. I have it here. I can submit it to you, and that is what is valid. All rights and responsibilities are derived from that. In our case, this was an attempt -- I was not aware of that decision. It was published -- I mean, the government gave it directly to Mr. Karadzic. And a state of war was never declared. That is why I draw your attention to this decision on the annulment of municipal commissioners, in view of what was stated here, along the lines of the non-existence of an expanded Presidency. Now I would like to try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try -- first of all, on -- I let you go, although a lot was repetitious, Mr. Krajisnik. But one thing you said -- you have drawn our attention to the decision of the annulment of municipal commissioners. Is that in evidence? Do you have that? Could you be a bit more specific about that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, the 17th of December at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the Assembly. At the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. The 17th of December we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's part of the agenda, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We, we have a tape-recording of that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the actual decision is in evidence, Your Honours, as one of the Hanson tabs, but I can double-check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that we can verify exactly the -- the importance of that decision. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a discussion here about the appointment of judges who were non-Serbs, Muslims, Yugoslavs, and Montenegrins. Montenegrins and Yugoslavs were not that much of a problem, but really the Muslims were. I tried to explain what the atmosphere was then at this session on the 12th of September. I just want to explain an additional thing to you, what significantly contributed to my understanding that this simply could not be carried through. All respectable judges, one of them was Marko Arsovic. He was a judge on the Muslim side of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was detained and had great trouble to flee to our territory, because on the other side people also did not allow members of other ethnic communities to try them. I thought about it later, too, whether I made a mistake, whether I made a mistake when I was thinking about this conclusion and whether it was correct. Had one single Muslim convicted one person for a crime, one Muslim judge, people would have said that that would have been on ethnic grounds. Mr. Karadzic tried to do this, appoint some people from Bijeljina, I have it here how many people were appointed. None of them came to take the solemn declaration, and quite simply this went down the drain. Ultimately, this was not a successful effort. Later on we thought that the climate would change and that perhaps the war would be brought to an end in due time. However, unfortunately, the climate did not change and ultimately there weren't any judges. But our position was that politically this was highly necessarily and proper from a human point of view but, quite simply, it could not be carried out. I would like to say something else now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have submitted some things to you here indicating the partiality of two witnesses. One from a humanitarian organisation and another one who is Mr. Okun. The first witness I referred to is a protected witness. I have provided documents for you here in terms of how they worked, how they changed their concepts. There is a CD here as well, I gave it to you, where Mr. Zimmerman himself admits that the Cutileiro Plan was a good one and that perhaps it could have been implemented and that he brought strong pressure to bear on Secretary Baker to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina. I provided this CD to you and you can see this statement of Mr. Zimmerman's there. Also this has to do with Mr. Okun who was present when they changed their concept to abolish Republika Srpska and to create regions. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although may I remind you that you are adding to the answers given as a witness and that this is not a time for argument. There will be ample opportunity to tell us how important this CD is and what we can see on it. I mean, I take it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's not specifically -- I wouldn't say that it's totally excluded from what a witness could tell us, but you as a witness, you brought us the CD. The importance of that will certainly be argued by counsel if they choose to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, it's certainly easy, we confess, to lose track of some of this material as we've all had this problem this morning. We're not immediately clear whether this CD that Mr. Krajisnik has just referred to is one of the ones that's in evidence or what it is. This -- Your Honour is absolutely right on the general point, but that supposes or presupposes that we can actually locate this material as already being in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all the -- Mr. Registrar has done already a lot of work to see what is in evidence and what is not in evidence. The Chamber, of course, is aware what problems this could cause to the parties. At the same time, it is all material that is in the possession, not only of this witness but of the accused as well, who perhaps at a later stage could assist you in identifying what is the importance of that material which was introduced through the witness. And of course the Chamber will consider if at any later stage where none of these documents have been adopted by one of the parties yet, if one of the parties would be tempted to tender them as contextual exhibits, the Chamber will certainly not have lost out of its mind at that moment the problems the parties are facing at this moment. Of course, I can't speak for my colleagues, but I know from the past experience that in these kind of matters we did show some flexibility on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour is understanding very well the marker that I just wanted to put down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I think you well understood my other statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further comment, Your Honour, understatement or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I provided that first CD, that big one -- actually, I gave two CDs. So I mean it's -- it was in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For me CDs are all of the same size, Mr. Krajisnik. Let's proceed. We'll try and identify what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to further assist counsel in this matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were complaints here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were complaints here, stating that we paid no attention to the reporting of foreign media and that we did not take into account what their reporting was. There is a document that I provided - it is there - how much the Muslim and Croat side paid various agencies, media, in order for them to report favourably about them. Only Muslim and Croat information could come through, not Serb information. You have that material. That's what I'm saying. There was a lack of confidence, and there was a lot of information that was obviously unfair and incorrect. I stated here that Sarajevo would be Serb if it is united, and I did not know the answer as to why I had stated that. I said exactly what it says there. The Prosecutor was right on that, but I know that my position was always that we should have part of Sarajevo rather than all of Sarajevo. I have provided you other documents, too. This was in 1994 at the time of the plan of the contact group. There was a blockade imposed by Serbia. At that time we were given the opportunity of establishing confederal links with Serbia. That is what was stated to the public by international mediators as well. International mediators came and offered exchanges of territories; it wasn't the Serb side. The Muslim side also asked for an exchange of territory: Muslim for Serb. Zepa, Srebrenica, Vogosca, and I don't know what other municipality was involved. I was against that, against us remaining without Sarajevo. I provided documents to you. Mr. Owen's book. I gave you this other gentleman: Cunning Strategies. Ah, Mr. Halilovic, yes. The third book written by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. So you have three documents. At that time they were considering exchanges of territories. I was against that, and their reason was to say that Sarajevo should be united -- or rather Muslim, in actual fact. And that was supposed to be their capital, the capital of their constituent unit. And then I said: All right. Let it be united but let it be Serb. That was a response to their aspiration. You will find that in Mr. Halilovic's book. They had a discussion about establishing a Muslim state, that is to say to have Bosnia divided. This was in 1994. So please, these are three documents that were important to show what kind of atmosphere existed why I said: "Well, if it's supposed to be united, let it be Serb," although that was not my position. And what I advocated throughout the interview was that the Serbs had a right to Sarajevo, too. Another thing I wish to indicate here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before you continue, we see that Mr. Krajisnik has some -- at least on the -- on the list I see, for example, already some references to, for example, Mr. Owen's book, which is only one out of the three mentioned by Mr. Krajisnik. Would the parties consider, since Mr. Krajisnik has referred to specific pages, whether they would object against those pages to be admitted into evidence more or less as contextual exhibits? I'm a bit hesitant, but I would like to know what the parties think about it. I'm hesitant for the following reason that tomorrow we have eight books of different authors all presenting their own views on the matter to be in evidence and for the Chamber not to deliver a judgement but a book review on seven or eight books. That's not, I think, the way we would go; at the same time, we invited Mr. Krajisnik to draw our attention to certain documents he considers to be important. So therefore, I'd like to have the view of the parties on it, but I have expressed already what might be a problem the Chamber would be facing, and therefore the parties are invited to include that, their positions, especially when we have not had a specific opportunity to deal with those portions of the book while examining the witness. Mr. Krajisnik, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I submitted Mr. Karadzic's letter to you. I don't insist on including the entire letter. I was just interested in one particular segment. He is the only person who knows 100 per cent whether an expanded Presidency exists -- existed. I sent a letter, through the investigator, and according to Rule 92 bis, as far as inaccessible persons are concerned, there are ways and means of -- I mean, it could be admitted in that way. I wanted to prove in that way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the statement or letter by Mr. Karadzic to the investigator is an issue on which we'll hear from the parties on whether it's admissible evidence, yes or no. I can assure you that Rule 92 bis is a bit more complex. If it were only that 92 bis, Rule 92 bis does not allow any evidence to be presented under that rule on the acts and conduct of the accused, the letter -- at least I could not exclude for the possibility that the letter directly deals with your acts and your conduct. Apart from that, Rule 92 bis requires some formalities to be fulfilled. And I can imagine that the Prosecution would cross-examine Mr. Karadzic on this statement, and I could not exclude for the possibility that such a request, if admissible and if Mr. Karadzic would be available, would be granted. So let's stay out of the 92 bis discussion at this moment which is, from a legal point of view, complex enough for the parties to deal with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right. I was just interested in that particular statement. I'm not interested in his entire statement. I just wanted to indicate why it was that I had proposed this. It's not about me; it's about the expanded Presidency. All right. I would like to indicate a general assessment that is very important. A countless number of questions were put to me: Did you learn of something? Did you take any measures? What did you do about that? And so on and so forth. I would like to indicate to the Trial Chamber that I did not have the right to punish anyone. I did not have the right to call anyone to be held accountable. I didn't have the right to promote anyone or to confer any decorations upon anyone. This has nothing to do with the subject matter of the expanded Presidency. I never did that -- I mean, even if it were to be understood that I was a member of some expanded Presidency, it did not mean that I was supposed to take some measures, taking advantage of that position. As much as I could as a person who took part in his own work, I did my work but I could not call someone in and say: I'm punishing you for this and that, I'm taking measures, and so on and so forth, because that was not within my authority. I could not do that. I could only take initiatives, support something, or complain if someone did not do something. That's what I did throughout. So when somebody says: What did you do about it? I could have done whatever any other citizen could have done. Had somebody told me a crime happened, I just could have made the government aware of this or the judiciary or whoever had I received such information. Of course I would have done that, had I known, but Djokanovic could have done it, too, and any other person. I'm trying to explain that I never did such a thing because it was not within my responsibilities. The Honourable Judge Hanoteau asked me whether I had the right to put something on the agenda of the Assembly, some initiative or something like that. As for our Assembly, every agenda had to have appropriate material. It was only when somebody was presenting some introductory remarks that that could be done only orally. Karadzic did it sometimes. It's not that somebody could say: Well, let's discuss a particular problem without any supporting material. As for any initiative that the president of the Assembly had, any MP or the government had the same right, but there was an exact separation of powers between the legislative, the judiciary, and the executive. Everybody did their own work. Now, the quality of their work was a different matter. But I accept everything that was done at the Assembly. If somebody were to ask me: Why did you do this? Why did you do that? You're guilty of this. You're guilty of that. That's only natural and I cannot explain what somebody did elsewhere and I cannot be held accountable of that in terms of whether they did this properly or whether the quality of their work was proper. I could just complain or voice some objections and that's what I did. There's been discussion here that I signed three documents about commissioners, Mr. Miskin, Mr. Mijatovic, and Mr. Jovanovic. I wish to indicate to the Trial Chamber that there were certificates, decisions, and rulings. The certificates that I signed for Mr. Jovanovic were of an earlier date -- or rather, before Mr. Koljevic was complaining about the fact that he could not control commissioners. Now, why did I sign this certificate for Karadzic? It was this. He had already been appointed, but he needed some sort of a certificate to be able to use this paper for whomever it may concern to certify that he was indeed a commissioner. That was during the time Mr. Koljevic was in charge of commissioners. I was probably there in the head office and he merely wanted this piece of paper which would enable him to go somewhere. You can double-check this. Mr. Miskin was the commissioner of the government. There are two documents. There are the minutes of the government meeting. Since the government seat was further away, he was asking for a certificate to be written, a piece of paper, so that people on the ground would be forthcoming in terms of providing him with fuel and other matters, and that is why I signed that paper. As far as Mr. Mijatovic is concerned, he substituted for Mr. Radovanovic and that was for just one day and then he returned. He was appointed by many Karadzic because the local commissioners didn't do their job. I wasn't in charge of commissioners because their work -- well, I did have contacts with MPs who were commissioners because I talked to them. This person that I talked to might have at the same time been commissioner. However, with those who were not MPs, I had no links with them whatsoever. I was not in charge of them, and I have now explained why these three signatures were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm looking at the clock. I think for additional matters we had half an hour in mind. And sometimes what you tell us is not exactly new and doesn't add very much, although sometimes it does. How much time you would think you would still need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best to finish shortly. I have three more items that I would like to discuss. There are more -- many more, but I would only talk about these three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I can look at the clock, you can't from there. It's eight minutes to 2.00. Would you please finish at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. I will and I hope I will finish even sooner than that. Mr. Kozic, I'm really sorry. Even now when I've been analysing these matters and I will be analysing the meeting held on the 20th of June, it wasn't my intention or it wasn't within my interest to conceal that Mr. Kozic was there. I have been trying to explain this, and I'm really sorry. I wouldn't wish to cover up for Kozic. Whatever I have stated about the matter reflected my memory of it. I'm really sorry that things turned the way they did, and I assure you that I tried to convey all my thoughts and my knowledge at the time. There is one subject -- another subject, which is that when ranking people in terms of their authority, it was always the order of Mr. Karadzic and then Mr. Krajisnik. Honourable Judges, I worked a lot. I had two roles that made me seem important to people. It's not that I had powers. First of all, I was running an Assembly within which everything was happening and the destiny of the people was people decided upon, and I attended negotiations. I had also that legacy of my previous work from the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I had repeatedly heard people say Karadzic and Krajisnik were important. And in fact, I never denied that. I never stated that I didn't have any powers because I did not want to disillusion people. But as I analysed my role, I had never really had any powers or authority. But in the eyes of people, I can say not that I wasn't important but the people placed their trust in me. But I never abused that, and I never used the position in order to order this or that and do that. And I never carried out other people's duties. I promised that finish, that's why I will touch upon one other subject. Davidovic. I don't want to repeat matters, but I would like to say the following to the Trial Chamber and my Defence counsel. There are statements concerning each of the matters that Mr. Davidovic mentioned when he accused Mr. Djurkovic, Mr. Vucic -- Mr. Vukovic, Mr. Micic. And there are statements of these people where they deny everything that Mr. Davidovic said. I, myself, cannot account at all for the fact that he stated these matters, save for one. During the war there was quite a lot of disinformation around. I read quite a few of them, and whatever was ideologically against me was taken for granted as such by him. I had never issued a decision referring to Mr. Djurkovic or I never -- or anything concerned Mr. Djurkovic, and you yourselves could see that. Perhaps this should be put under Rule 92 bis to have these statements of these people admitted. I have been mentioning this on several occasions, but there is no time for me to go into this matter. But if I will have the time, I will try to clear my face with regard to these accusations. Your Honours, I have no more time, that's why I will finish here. So I did finish one minute earlier than 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. From my point of view even two. I think it's the right thing to do at this very moment, also because you anticipated already in your last comments on your change of position, which will be a change of position from now on, that is that you're again the accused and not a witness anymore. Just for practical matters, would the parties -- we need a break anyhow at this moment. One of the important things we still have to do is deal with all of the exhibits. We could try and do that in a rush immediately after the break. We could also try and do it once we have sorted out a few matters such as these provisionally assigned numbers, when the parties have had an opportunity perhaps to view again at the -- at the CD what is on it. I'm wondering whether we should continue today with these kind of matters or whether we would leave them for a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've been working on the exhibits, and I'm certainly going to object to a number. My rough estimate is my submission will take 15 minutes. That is a very rough estimate. Of course it -- well, let -- could I also mention that Mr. Stewart has some other procedural matters that he would like to raise at some juncture today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Speaking for him, if I may, I suspect they'll take about 10 to 15 minutes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can't speak to the timing or necessity of the procedural matters, but insofar as the exhibits are concerned, Prosecution takes the Court's point. If -- in particular it seems to me that if the Defence has objections to a certain number of exhibits, particularly objections that we haven't discussed previously, it would be of some benefit in terms of the time spent in court to identify all of the exhibits at issue, including provisional ones or those that otherwise hadn't been brought to the parties' attention before, and insofar as possible determine the extent to which some accord exists or the arguments to the extent they may exist can be narrowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is a suggestion now made by Mr. Tieger that you would try and exchange views on the admissibility of some of the evidence and to see whether matters can be resolved, yes or no. Mr. Josse, would that be something that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got no objection to that. Indeed it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I take it that under the communication the communication blockade would be not -- would be stopped from this moment. I take it the issues you would like to discuss would be legal issues and if you would be in a position to speak with Mr. Krajisnik it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right to say that -- yes, that is correct. In fact, Your Honour has anticipated another issue which is we are anxious to speak to Mr. Krajisnik as soon as possible. Indeed, I think before Mr. Stewart raises his matters we would like to speak to Mr. Krajisnik. As far as the exhibit issue is concerned, we don't really need to speak to Mr. Krajisnik. It's simply the logistics of this because probably the best thing to do would be for me to have a short meeting with my learned friend, Mr. Tieger, a matter of finding the time to do that, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I do understand you well that there's no objection against any evidentiary issue prior to making objections before the Chamber. This would allow Mr. Registrar also perhaps to earmark some of the exhibits which have been slipped in more or less in the earlier days of Mr. Krajisnik's testimony where they were assigned exhibit numbers, many of them perhaps already in evidence. So to have that all sorted out before we finally come to raising objections that remain and before deciding on the admission of this evidence. So that would be -- so then we have -- then I do understand. Mr. Stewart, you have -- you wanted to raise a few procedural issues of a different character, but you would like to speak with Mr. Krajisnik before raising them. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we wanted to be clear, as Mr. Josse just indicated. Mr. Krajisnik has now officially finished as a witness, has he, and we are -- normal communication is resumed. Then we would like to go and see him in this imminent break, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that is the position of the Prosecution as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Insofar as I understand the situation at the moment, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- because we are limited on our time Mr. Josse indicated that you would need approximately ten minutes to raise the matter. I don't know of course what the character of is it. I don't know whether there would be any response or not. I would like to have a short break of approximately 20 minutes, and I would like to finish for the day not later than quarter to, ten minutes to 3.00. I know it's short, but it's a bit of an unusual day for the Chamber, not only because of dentists. Then -- but I'd like now to turn into private session for one second before we have that break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it's just one area, Your Honour, the practical matters, but it would require the Trial Chamber to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything to be raised by the parties in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nothing else from the Defence today. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
